text:
Let y = y(x) be the solution of the differential equation 

$\frac{dy}{dx}=(y+1)\left ((y+1)e^{x^{2}/2}-x\right )$, 0 < x < 2.1, with y(2) = 0. Then the value of $\frac{dy}{dx}$ at x = 1 is equal to :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2021 (Online) 18th March Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
$\frac{dy}{dx}=(y+1)\left ((y+1)e^{\frac{x2}{2}}-x\right )$

$\Rightarrow \frac{-1}{(y+1)^{2}}\frac{dy}{dx}-x\left (\frac{1}{y+1}\right )=-e^{\frac{x2}{2}}$

Put, $\frac{1}{y+1}=z$

$-\frac{1}{(y+1)^{2}}.\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{dz}{dx}$

$\therefore$ $\frac{dz}{dx}+z(-x)=-e^{\frac{x2}{2}}$

$I.F=e^{\int -xdx}=e^{\frac{-x2}{2}}$

$z.\left (e^{-\frac{x2}{2}}\right )=-\int e^{-\frac{x2}{2}}.e^{\frac{x2}{2}}dx=-\int 1.dx=-x+C$

$\Rightarrow \frac{e^{-\dfrac{x2}{2}}}{y+1}=-x+C$ .... (1)

Given y = 0 at x = 2 Put in (1)

$\frac{e^{-2}}{0+1}=-2+C$

$C=e^{-2}+2$ .... (2)

From (1) and (2)

$y+1=\frac{e^{-\dfrac{x2}{2}}}{e^{-2}+2-x}$

Again, at x = 1

$\Rightarrow y+1=\frac{e^{3/2}}{e^{2}+1}$

$\Rightarrow y+1=\frac{e^{3/2}}{e^{2}+1}$

$\therefore$ $\frac{dy}{dx}\left |_{x=1}=\frac{e^{3/2}}{e^{2}+1}\left (\frac{e^{3/2}}{e^{2}+1}\times e^{1/2}-1\right ) \right.$

$=-\frac{e^{3/2}}{(e^{2}+1)^{2}}$
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2021 (Online) 18th March Evening Shift

text:
Let the system of linear equations 

4x + $λ$y + 2z = 0

2x $-$ y + z = 0

$μ$x + 2y + 3z = 0, $λ$, $μ\in$R.

has a non-trivial solution. Then which of the following is true?
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2021 (Online) 18th March Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Given, system of linear equations

4x + $λ$y + 2z = 0

2x $-$ y + z = 0

$μ$x + 2y + 3z = 0

For non-trivial solution, $\Delta$ = 0

$\left |\begin{array}{lll} 4 & λ & 2 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 \\ μ & 2 & 3 \end{array}\right |=0$

$\Rightarrow 4(-3-2)-λ(6-μ)+2(4+μ)=0$

$\Rightarrow -λ(6-μ)-2(6-μ)=0$

$\Rightarrow (6-μ)(λ+2)=0$

$\Rightarrow λ=-2$ and $μ\in R$ or $μ$ = 6 and $λ\in R$.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2021 (Online) 18th March Evening Shift

text: The area bounded by the curve $4y^{2} = x^{2}(4$ $-$ x)(x $-$ 2) is equal to :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2021 (Online) 18th March Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Given,

$4y^{2} = x^{2}(4$ $-$ x)(x $-$ 2) ..... (1)

Here, Left hand side $4y^{2}$ is always positive. So Right hand side should also be positive.

In x$\in$ [2, 4] Right hand side is positive.

By putting y = $-$y in equation (1), equation remains same. So, graph is symmetric about x axis.

 
[IMG]
 

Required Area $= 2A_{1}$

$=2\int\limits _{2}^{4}ydx$

$=\int\limits _{2}^{4}x\sqrt{(x-2)(4-x)}dx$

put $x=4\sin ^{2}θ+2\cos ^{2}θ$

$\Rightarrow dx=[8\sin θ\cos θ-4\sin θ\cos θ]dθ$

$\Rightarrow dx=4\sin θ\cos θdθ$

When lower limit = 2 then 

$2=4\sin ^{2}θ+2\cos ^{2}θ$

$\Rightarrow 4(1-\cos ^{2}θ)+2\cos ^{2}θ=2$

$\Rightarrow 4-4\cos ^{2}θ+2\cos ^{2}θ=2$

$\Rightarrow 2\cos ^{2}θ=2$

$\Rightarrow \cos θ=\pm 1$

$\Rightarrow θ=0,π$

When upper limit = 4 then

$4=4\sin ^{2}θ+2\cos ^{2}θ$

$\Rightarrow -2\cos ^{2}θ=0$

$\Rightarrow θ=\frac{π~}{2}$

$\therefore$ Range of $θ$ = 0 to $\frac{π~}{2}$

$\therefore$ Area = $\int\limits _{0}^{\frac{π\; }{2}}(4\sin ^{2}θ+2\cos ^{2}θ)\sqrt{(2\sin ^{2}θ)(2\cos ^{2}θ)}(4\sin θ\cos θ)dθ$

$=\int\limits _{0}^{\frac{π\; }{2}}(4\sin ^{2}θ+2\cos ^{2}θ)8\sin ^{2}θ\cos ^{2}θdθ$

$=32\int\limits _{0}^{\frac{π\; }{2}}\sin ^{4}θ\cos ^{2}θdθ+16\int\limits _{0}^{\frac{π\; }{2}}\sin ^{2}θ\cos ^{4}θdθ$

Using Wallis formula,

$=32.\frac{3.1.1}{6.4.2}.\frac{π~}{2}+16.\frac{1.3.1}{6.4.2}.\frac{π~}{2}$

$=π+\frac{π~}{2}$

$=\frac{3π}{2}$

If $15\sin ^{4}α$ $+ 10\cos ^{4}α$ = 6, for some $α\in$R, then the value of 

$27\sec ^{6}α$ + 8cosec$^{6}α$ is equal to :

solution.body: $\begin{array}{l} \text{Given,}15\sin ^{4}α+10\cos ^{4}α=6 \\  \\ \Rightarrow 15\sin ^{4}α+10\cos ^{4}α=6\left (\sin ^{2}α+\cos ^{2}α\right )^{2} \\  \\ \Rightarrow 15\sin ^{4}α+10\cos ^{4}α=6\left (\sin ^{4}α+\cos ^{4}α+2\sin ^{2}α\cos ^{2}α\right ) \\  \\ \Rightarrow 9\sin ^{4}α+4\cos ^{4}α-12\sin ^{2}α\cos ^{2}α=0 \\  \\ \Rightarrow \left (3\sin ^{2}α-2\cos ^{2}α\right )^{2}=0 \\  \\ \Rightarrow 3\sin ^{2}α-2\cos ^{2}α=0 \\  \\ \Rightarrow 3\sin ^{2}α=2\cos ^{2}α \\  \\ \Rightarrow \tan ^{2}α=2/3 \\  \\ \therefore \quad \cot ^{2}α=3/2 \\  \\ \text{Now,}27\sec ^{6}α+8\mathrm{cosec}^{6}α=27\left (\sec ^{2}α\right )^{3}+8\left (\mathrm{cosec}^{2}α\right )^{3} \\  \\ =27\left (1+\tan ^{2}α\right )^{3}+8\left (1+\cot ^{2}α\right )^{3} \\  \\ =27\left (1+\dfrac{2}{3}\right )^{3}+8\left (1+\dfrac{3}{2}\right )^{3}=250 \end{array}$

text: Let $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ be two non-zero vectors perpendicular to each other and $|\vec{a}|=|\vec{b}|$. If $|\vec{a}\times \vec{b}|=|\vec{a}|$, then the angle between the vectors $\left (\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\left (\vec{a}\times \vec{b}\right )\right )$ and $\vec{a}$ is equal to :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2021 (Online) 18th March Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
$\vec{a}$ is perpendicular to $\vec{b}$

$\therefore$ $\vec{a}$ . $\vec{b}$ = 0

Given, | $\vec{a}$ $\times$ $\vec{b}$ | = | $\vec{a}$ |

and | $\vec{a}$ | = | $\vec{b}$ |

$\therefore$ | $\vec{a}$ $\times$ $\vec{b}$ | = | $\vec{a}$ | = | $\vec{b}$ | = k(assume)

Now, angle between $\vec{a}$ and ($\vec{a}$ + $\vec{b}$ + ($\vec{a}$ $\times$ $\vec{b}$))

$\cos θ=\frac{\vec{a}((\vec{a}+\vec{b}+(\vec{a}\times \vec{b}))}{|\vec{a}|.|\vec{a}+\vec{b}+(\vec{a}\times \vec{b})|}$

$=\frac{|\vec{a}|^{2}+\vec{a}.\vec{b}+\vec{a}(\vec{a}\times \vec{b})}{|\vec{a}|.|\vec{a}+\vec{b}+(\vec{a}\times \vec{b})|}$

[Note $\vec{a}.(\vec{a}\times \vec{b})=[\vec{a}\vec{a}\vec{b}]=0$]

$=\frac{|\vec{a}|^{2}+0+0}{|\vec{a}|.|\vec{a}+\vec{b}+(\vec{a}\times \vec{b})|}$

Now, $|\vec{a}+\vec{b}+(\vec{a}\times \vec{b})|^{2}$

$=|\vec{a}|^{2}+|\vec{a}|^{2}+|\vec{a}\times \vec{b}|^{2}+$

$2\vec{a}.\vec{b}+2\vec{b}.(\vec{a}\times \vec{b})+2\vec{a}.(\vec{a}\times \vec{b})$

$=k^{2}+k^{2}+k^{2}$

$\therefore$ $|\vec{a}+\vec{b}+(\vec{a}\times \vec{b})|^{2}=3k^{2}$

$\Rightarrow |\vec{a}+\vec{b}+(\vec{a}\times \vec{b})|=\sqrt{3}k$

$\therefore$ $\cos θ=\frac{k^{2}}{k(\sqrt{3}k)}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$

$\Rightarrow θ=\cos ^{-1}\left (\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right )$

text:
Let f : R $\to$ R be a function defined as

$f(x)=\left \{\begin{array}{l} \frac{\sin (a+1)x+\sin 2x}{2x},ifx<0 \\ b,if\qquad x=0 \\ \frac{\sqrt{x+bx^{3}}-\sqrt{x}}{bx^{5/2}},ifx>0 \end{array} \right.$

If f is continuous at x = 0, then the value of a + b is equal to :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2021 (Online) 18th March Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Given, $f(x)=\left \{\begin{array}{ll} \frac{\sin (a+1)x+\sin 2x}{2x}, & x<0 \\ b, & x=0 \\ \frac{\sqrt{x+bx^{3}}-\sqrt{x}}{bx^{5/2}}, & x>0 \end{array} \right.$

$\begin{array}{ll} \because  & f(x)\text{is continuous at}x=0. \\  \\ \therefore  & \lim _{x\to 0^{-}}f(x)=\lim _{x\to 0^{+}}f(x)=f(0) \\  \\ \because  & f(0)=b \end{array}$

Now, $\lim _{x\to 0^{-}}f(x)=\lim _{x\to 0^{-}}\left (\frac{\sin (a+1)x+\sin 2x}{2x}\right )$

$\begin{array}{ll} \Rightarrow \quad \lim _{x\to 0^{-}}f(x) & =\lim _{x\to 0^{-}}\left (\dfrac{\sin (a+1)x}{2x}+\dfrac{\sin 2x}{2x}\right ) \\  \\ =\lim _{x\to 0^{-}}\left (\dfrac{\sin (a+1)x}{(a+1)x}\times \left (\dfrac{a+1}{2}\right )+\dfrac{\sin 2x}{2x}\right ) \\  \\ =\dfrac{a+1}{2}+1 \end{array}$

Again, $\lim _{x\to 0^{+}}f(x)=\lim _{x\to 0^{+}}\left (\frac{\sqrt{x+bx^{3}}-\sqrt{x}}{bx^{5/2}}\right )$

$=\lim _{x\to 0^{+}}\frac{\left (\sqrt{x+bx^{3}}-\sqrt{x}\right )\left (\sqrt{x+bx^{3}}+\sqrt{x}\right )}{bx^{5/2}\left (\sqrt{x+bx^{3}}+\sqrt{x}\right )}$

$\begin{array}{l} =\lim _{x\to 0^{+}}\dfrac{\left (x+bx^{3}-x\right )}{bx^{5/2}\left (\sqrt{x+bx^{3}}+\sqrt{x}\right )} \\  \\ =\lim _{x\to 0^{+}}\dfrac{\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{x}\left (\sqrt{1+bx^{2}}+1\right )} \end{array}$

$\Rightarrow \quad \lim _{x\to 0^{+}}f(x)=1/2$

From Eq. (i), (ii), (iii) and (iv)

$\begin{array}{l} \dfrac{1}{2}=b=\dfrac{a+1}{2}+1\Rightarrow b=\dfrac{1}{2},a=-2 \\  \\ \therefore \quad a+b=\dfrac{-3}{2} \end{array}$
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2021 (Online) 18th March Evening Shift

text: Let g(x) = $\int\limits _{0}^{x}f(t)dt$, where f is continuous function in [ 0, 3 ] such that $\frac{1}{3}$ $\leq$ f(t) $\leq$ 1 for all t$\in$ [0, 1] and 0 $\leq$ f(t) $\leq$ $\frac{1}{2}$ for all t$\in$ (1, 3]. The largest possible interval in which g(3) lies is :

solution.body:
Given, $g(x)=\int\limits _{0}^{x}f(t)dt$

$\therefore g(3)=\int\limits _{0}^{3}f(t)dt=\int\limits _{0}^{1}f(t)dt+\int\limits _{1}^{3}f(t)dt$

$\Rightarrow \int\limits _{0}^{1}\frac{1}{3}dt+\int\limits _{1}^{3}0\cdot dt\leq g(3)\leq \int\limits _{0}^{1}1dt+\int\limits _{1}^{3}\frac{1}{2}dt$

$\Rightarrow \frac{1}{3}\leq g(3)\leq 1+1$

$\Rightarrow \frac{1}{3}\leq g(3)\leq 2$

text: Let in a series of 2n observations, half of them are equal to a and remaining half are equal to $-$a. Also by adding a constant b in each of these observations, the mean and standard deviation of new set become 5 and 20, respectively. Then the value of $a^{2} + b^{2}$ is equal to :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2021 (Online) 18th March Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Given series

(a, a, a, ........ n times), ($-$a, $-$a, $-$a, ...... n times)

Now $x–$ = $\frac{\sum x_{i}}{2n}=0$

as, $x_{i}$ $\to$ $x_{i} + b$

then $x–$ $\to$ $x–$ + b

So, $x–$ + b = 5 $\Rightarrow$ b = 5

No change in S.D. due to change in origin

Standard deviation ($σ$) = $\sqrt{\frac{\sum\limits _{i=1}^{2n}(x_{i}-x–)^{2}}{2n}}$

$=\sqrt{\frac{\sum\limits _{i=1}^{2n}x_{i}^{2}}{2n}}=\sqrt{\frac{2na^{2}}{2n}}=\sqrt{a^{2}}$

$\therefore$ $20=\sqrt{a^{2}}\Rightarrow a=20$

$\therefore$ $a^{2} + b^{2} = 425$
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2021 (Online) 18th March Evening Shift

text:
Define a relation R over a class of n $\times$ n real matrices A and B as 

"ARB iff there exists a non-singular matrix P such that PAP$^{-1} = B$". 

Then which of the following is true?
options: R is reflexive, transitive but not symmetric
R is symmetric, transitive but not reflexive.
R is reflexive, symmetric but not transitive
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2021 (Online) 18th March Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
For reflexive relation,

 $\forall (A,A)\in R$ for matrix $P$.

$\Rightarrow A=PAP^{-1}$ is true for $P=I$

So, $R$ is reflexive relation.

For symmetric relation,

Let $(A,B)\in R$ for matrix $P$.

$\Rightarrow \quad A=PBP^{-1}$

After pre-multiply by $P^{-1}$ and post-multiply by $P$, we get

$P^{-1}AP=B$

So, $(B,A)\in R$ for matrix $P^{-1}$.

So, $R$ is a symmetric relation.

For transitive relation,

Let $ARB$ and $BRC$

So, $A=PBP^{-1}$ and $B=PCP^{-1}$

Now, $A=P\left (PCP^{-1}\right )P^{-1}$

$\Rightarrow A=(P)^{2}C\left (P^{-1}\right )^{2}\Rightarrow A=(P)^{2}\cdot C\cdot \left (P^{2}\right )^{-1}$

$\therefore (A,C)\in R$ for matrix $P^{2}$.

$\therefore R$ is transitive relation.

Hence, $R$ is an equivalence relation.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2021 (Online) 18th March Evening Shift

text:
Let f : R $-$ {3} $\to$ R $-$ {1} be defined by f(x) = $\frac{x-2}{x-3}$.

Let g : R $\to$ R be given as g(x) = 2x $-$ 3. Then, the sum of all the values of x for which $f^{-1}(x) + g^{-1}(x) =$ $\frac{13}{2}$ is equal to :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2021 (Online) 18th March Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Finding inverse of f(x)

$y=\frac{x-2}{x-3}\Rightarrow xy-3y=x-2\Rightarrow x(y-1)=3y-2$

$\therefore$ $f^{-1}(x)=\frac{3x-2}{x-1}$

Similarly for $g^{-1}(x)$

$y=2x-3\Rightarrow x=\frac{y+3}{2}\Rightarrow g^{-1}(x)=\frac{x+3}{2}$

$\therefore$ $\frac{3x-2}{x-1}+\frac{x+3}{2}=\frac{13}{2}$

$\Rightarrow 6x-4+x^{2}+2x-3=13x-13$

$\Rightarrow x^{2}-5x+6=0$

$\Rightarrow (x-2)(x-3)=0$

$\Rightarrow$ x = 2 or 3

text: If f(x) and g(x) are two polynomials such that the polynomial $P(x) = f(x^{3}) + x g(x^{3})$ is divisible by $x^{2} + x + 1$, then P(1) is equal to $___________$.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2021 (Online) 18th March Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Given, $p(x) = f(x^{3}) + xg(x^{3})$

We know, $x^{2} + x + 1 = (x$ $-$ $ω$) (x $-$ $ω^{2}$)

Given, p(x) is divisible by $x^{2} + x + 1$. So, roots of p(x) is $ω$ and $ω^{2}$.

As root satisfy the equation,

So, put x = $ω$

p($ω$) = f($ω^{3}$) + $ω$g($ω^{3}$) = 0

= f(1) + $ω$g(1) = 0 [$ω^{3}$ = 1]

= f(1) + $\left (-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{i\sqrt{3}}{2}\right )$ g(1) = 0

$\Rightarrow$ f(1) $-$ $\frac{g(1)}{2}+i\left (\frac{\sqrt{3}g(1)}{2}\right )$ = 0 + i0

Comparing both sides, we get

f(1) $-$ $\frac{g(1)}{2}$ = 0

and $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}g(1)=0$ $\Rightarrow$ g(1) = 0

So, f(1) = 0

Now, p(1) = f(1) + 1 . g(1) = 0 + 0 = 0

text:
The term independent of x in the expansion of 

$\left [\frac{x+1}{x^{2/3}-x^{1/3}+1}-\frac{x-1}{x-x^{1/2}}\right ]^{10}$, x $\neq$ 1, is equal to $____________$.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2021 (Online) 18th March Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
$\left (\frac{x+1}{x^{2/3}-x^{1/3}+1}-\frac{x-1}{x-x^{1/2}}\right )^{10}$

= $\left (\frac{\left (x^{1/3}\right )^{3}+\left (1^{1/3}\right )^{3}}{x^{2/3}-x^{1/3}+1}-\frac{\left (\sqrt{x}\right )^{2}-(1)^{2}}{x-x^{1/2}}\right )^{10}$

= $\left (\frac{\left (x^{1/3}+1\right )\left (x^{2/3}-x^{1/3}+1\right )}{x^{2/3}-x^{1/3}+1}-\frac{\left (\sqrt{x}+1\right )\left (\sqrt{x}-1\right )}{\sqrt{x}\left (\sqrt{x}-1\right )}\right )^{10}$

= $\left (\left (x^{1/3}+1\right )-\frac{\left (\sqrt{x}+1\right )}{\sqrt{x}}\right )^{10}$

= $\left (\left (x^{1/3}+1\right )-\left (1+\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\right )\right )^{10}$

= $\left (x^{1/3}-\frac{1}{x^{1/2}}\right )^{10}$

$T_{r+1}={}^{10}C_{r}\left (x^{\frac{1}{3}}\right )^{(10-r)}\left (x^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right )^{r}$

For being independent of $x:\frac{10-r}{3}-\frac{r}{2}=0\Rightarrow r=4$

Term independent of $x={}^{10}C_{4}=210$

text:
Let y = y(x) be the solution of the differential equation 

xdy $-$ ydx = $\sqrt{(x^{2}-y^{2})}dx$, x $\geq$ 1, with y(1) = 0. If the area bounded by the line $x = 1, x = e^{π}, y = 0$ and y = y(x) is $αe^{2π} +$ $β$, then the value of 10($α$ + $β$) is equal to $__________$.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2021 (Online) 18th March Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
$xdy-ydx=\sqrt{x^{2}-y^{2}}dx$

dividing both sides by $x^{2}$, we get

$\frac{xdy-ydx}{x^{2}}=\frac{\sqrt{x^{2}-y^{2}}}{x^{2}}dx$

$\Rightarrow d\left (\frac{y}{x}\right )=\frac{1}{x}\sqrt{1-\left (\frac{y}{x}\right )^{2}}dx$

$\Rightarrow \frac{d\left (\frac{y}{x}\right )}{\sqrt{1-\left (\frac{y}{x}\right )^{2}}}=\frac{dx}{x}$

Integrating both side, we get

$\Rightarrow \int \frac{d\left (\frac{y}{x}\right )}{\sqrt{1-\left (\frac{y}{x}\right )^{2}}}=\int \frac{dx}{x}$

$\sin ^{-1}\left (\frac{y}{x}\right )=\ln (x)+C$

Given, y(1) = 0 $\Rightarrow$ at x = 1, y = 0

$\therefore$ $\Rightarrow \sin ^{-1}(0)=\ln (1)+C$

$\Rightarrow$ C = 0

$\therefore$ $\sin ^{-1}\left (\frac{y}{x}\right )=\ln (x)$

$\Rightarrow$ y = x sin(ln(x))

$\therefore$ Area $=\int\limits _{1}^{e^{π\; }}x\sin (\ln (x))dx$

Let, lnx = t

$\Rightarrow$ $x = e^{t}$

$\Rightarrow$ $dx = e^{t} dt$

New lower limit, t = ln(1) = 0

and upper limit t = ln$(e^{π~})$ = $π$

$\therefore$ Area = $\int\limits _{0}^{{}^{π\; }}e^{t}\sin (t).e^{t}dt$

$=\int\limits _{0}^{{}^{π\; }}e^{2t}\sin tdt$

$=\left [\frac{e^{2t}}{(1^{2}+2^{2})}(2\sin t-1\cos t)\right ]_{0}^{π~}$

$=\left [\frac{e^{2π}}{5}(0-(-1))-\frac{1}{5}(-1)\right ]$

$=\frac{e^{2π}}{5}+\frac{1}{5}$

$=αe^{2π}+β$

$\therefore$ $α=\frac{1}{5},β=\frac{1}{5}$

So, $10(α+β)=4$

text: Let I be an identity matrix of order 2 $\times$ 2 and P = $\left [\begin{array}{ll} 2 & -1 \\ 5 & -3 \end{array}\right ]$. Then the value of n$\in$N for which $P^{n} = 5I$ $-$ 8P is equal to $____________$.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2021 (Online) 18th March Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
$P=\left [\begin{array}{ll} 2 & -1 \\ 5 & -3 \end{array}\right ]$

$\left |\begin{array}{ll} 2-λ & -1 \\ 5 & -3-λ \end{array}\right |=0$

$\Rightarrow$ $λ^{2}$ + $λ$ $-$ 1 = 0

$\Rightarrow$ $P^{2} + P$ $-$ I = 0

$\Rightarrow$ $P^{2} = I$ $-$ P

$\Rightarrow$ $P^{4} = I + P^{2}$ $-$ 2P

$\Rightarrow$ $P^{4} = 2I$ $-$ 3P

Now, $P^{4} . P^{2} = (2I$ $-$ 3P)(I $-$ P) = 2I $-$ $5P + 3P^{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $P^{6} = 5I$ $-$ 8P

So n = 6

text:
Let f : R $\to$ R satisfy the equation f(x + y) = f(x) . f(y) for all x, y $\in$R and f(x) $\neq$ 0 for any x$\in$R. If the function f is differentiable at x = 0 and f'(0) = 3, then 

$\lim _{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}(f(h)-1)$ is equal to $____________$.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2021 (Online) 18th March Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Given, $f(x+y)=f(x).f(y)\forall x,y\in R$

$\therefore$ $f(x)=a^{x}\Rightarrow f^{'}(x)=a^{x}.\log (a)$

Now, $f^{'}(0)=\log (a)\Rightarrow 3=\log (a)\Rightarrow a=e^{3}$

$\therefore$ $f(x)=(e^{3})^{x}=e^{3x}$

$\therefore$ $f(h)=e^{3h}$

Now, $\lim _{h\to 0}\left (\frac{f(h)-1}{h}\right )=\lim _{h\to 0}\left (\frac{e^{3h}-1}{h}\right )$

$=\lim _{h\to 0}\left (\frac{e^{3h}-1}{3h}\times 3\right )=3\times 1=3$
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2021 (Online) 18th March Evening Shift

text: Let P(x) be a real polynomial of degree 3 which vanishes at x = $-$3. Let P(x) have local minima at x = 1, local maxima at x = $-$1 and $\int\limits _{-1}^{1}P(x)dx$ = 18, then the sum of all the coefficients of the polynomial P(x) is equal to $_________$.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2021 (Online) 18th March Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
P'(x) = a(x + 1)(x $-$ 1)

$\therefore$ P(x) = $\frac{ax^{3}}{3}$ $-$ ax + C

P($-$3) = 0 (given)

$\Rightarrow$ a($-$9 + 3) + C = 0

$\Rightarrow$ 6a = C ..... (i)

Also, $\int\limits _{-1}^{1}P(x)dx=18$

$\Rightarrow \int\limits _{-1}^{1}\left (a\left (\frac{x^{3}}{3}-x\right )+C\right )dx=18$

$\Rightarrow 0+2C=18\Rightarrow C=9$

from (i)

$a=\frac{3}{2}$

$\therefore$ $P(x)=\frac{x^{3}}{2}-\frac{3}{2}x+9$

Sum of co-efficient

 = $\frac{1}{2}-\frac{3}{2}+9$ = $-$1 + 9 = 8
